dmm-2018-power-02a.title: Count prime factors
dmm-2018-power-02a.body:
$50400=2^5\cdot3^2\cdot5^2\cdot7$ has $5+2+2+1=10$ prime factors counted with multiplicity. Each ratio $k_i\ge2$ uses up at least one of them, so there are at most $10$ ratios and $n\le11$. Equality is attained with $a_1=1$ and the ratios being the $10$ primes in any order.

**Answer: 11**

dmm-2018-power-02b.title: Orderings of the prime factors
dmm-2018-power-02b.body:
The longest length is $k=11$ (previous part), and then $a_1=1$ and the $10$ ratios are exactly the prime factors of $50400=2^5\cdot3^2\cdot5^2\cdot7$ in some order, and different orders give different sequences. The number of orders is $\frac{10!}{5!\,2!\,2!\,1!}=\frac{3628800}{480}=7560$.

**Answer: 7560**

dmm-2018-power-03.title: Recursion over divisors
dmm-2018-power-03.body:
Let $f(m)$ be the number of SG sequences with last term $m$. Such a sequence is either $(m)$ alone, or has a previous term $d$, a proper divisor of $m$, followed by $m$ (the ratio $m/d\ge2$ is automatic). So $f(m)=1+\sum_{d\mid m,\,d<m}f(d)$, and $f$ depends only on the prime signature of $m$. Writing $p,q,r,s$ for distinct primes:

$f(1)=1$, $f(p)=2$, $f(p^2)=1+1+2=4$, $f(pq)=1+1+2+2=6$, $f(p^2q)=1+(1+2+2+4+6)=16$, $f(pqr)=1+(1+3\cdot2+3\cdot6)=26$, $f(p^2qr)=1+(1+2+4+4+12+6+32+26)=88$, $f(pqrs)=1+(1+4\cdot2+6\cdot6+4\cdot26)=150$.

For $420=2^2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7$ the proper divisors are $2^a\cdot(\text{a product of }j\text{ of }3,5,7)$. Summing $f$ over them: for $a=0$: $1\cdot1+3\cdot2+3\cdot6+1\cdot26=51$; for $a=1$: $1\cdot2+3\cdot6+3\cdot26+1\cdot150=248$; for $a=2$ (excluding $420$ itself): $1\cdot4+3\cdot16+3\cdot88=316$. So $f(420)=1+51+248+316=616$.

**Answer: 616**

dmm-2018-power-04a.title: Bounds
dmm-2018-power-04a.body:
**Basic fact.** If an SG sequence of length $m$ has ratios $k_i=a_{i+1}/a_i\ge2$, its sum is $a_1S$ with $S=1+k_1+k_1k_2+\dots+k_1\cdots k_{m-1}=1+k_1\,(1+k_2+k_2k_3+\cdots)$. So $S=1+k_1S'$ where $S'$ is the same quantity for the tail $a_2,\dots,a_m$ (length $m-1$). Since all $k_i\ge2$, $S\ge1+2+\dots+2^{m-1}=2^m-1$; in particular **a sequence of length $m$ has sum at least $2^m-1$.** Conversely, $n$ has an SG sequence of length $m$ iff $n=a_1S$ for such an $S$.

A sequence of length $5$ has sum at least $2^5-1=31>19$, so $\sigma(19)\le4$. The sequence $1,2,4,12$ (ratios $2,2,3$) has sum $19$ and length $4$. So $\sigma(19)=4$.

**Answer: 4**

dmm-2018-power-04b.title: Rule out length 4
dmm-2018-power-04b.body:
**Basic fact.** If an SG sequence of length $m$ has ratios $k_i=a_{i+1}/a_i\ge2$, its sum is $a_1S$ with $S=1+k_1+k_1k_2+\dots+k_1\cdots k_{m-1}=1+k_1\,(1+k_2+k_2k_3+\cdots)$. So $S=1+k_1S'$ where $S'$ is the same quantity for the tail $a_2,\dots,a_m$ (length $m-1$). Since all $k_i\ge2$, $S\ge1+2+\dots+2^{m-1}=2^m-1$; in particular **a sequence of length $m$ has sum at least $2^m-1$.** Conversely, $n$ has an SG sequence of length $m$ iff $n=a_1S$ for such an $S$.

Note that for length $3$, $S=1+k_1(1+k_2)$ with $k_1\ge2$, $1+k_2\ge3$, so $S-1$ must be a **composite** number written as a product of a factor $\ge2$ and a factor $\ge3$; in particular $S-1$ is never prime.

Length $5$ needs sum $\ge31>25$. Length $3$ is possible: $1,4,20$ (ratios $4,5$) has sum $25$.

Suppose a length-$4$ SG sequence has sum $25=a_1S$ with $S\ge15$. Then $S\mid25$ forces $S=25$, $a_1=1$, and $24=k_1S'$ where $S'\ge7$ is the value for a length-$3$ tail, so $S'\in\{12,8\}$ (the divisors of $24$ that are $\ge7$, with $k_1=2,3$). But $S'-1\in\{11,7\}$ is prime, contradicting the composite requirement for length $3$. So $\sigma(25)=3$.

**Answer: 3**

dmm-2018-power-04c.title: Bounds
dmm-2018-power-04c.body:
**Basic fact.** If an SG sequence of length $m$ has ratios $k_i=a_{i+1}/a_i\ge2$, its sum is $a_1S$ with $S=1+k_1+k_1k_2+\dots+k_1\cdots k_{m-1}=1+k_1\,(1+k_2+k_2k_3+\cdots)$. So $S=1+k_1S'$ where $S'$ is the same quantity for the tail $a_2,\dots,a_m$ (length $m-1$). Since all $k_i\ge2$, $S\ge1+2+\dots+2^{m-1}=2^m-1$; in particular **a sequence of length $m$ has sum at least $2^m-1$.** Conversely, $n$ has an SG sequence of length $m$ iff $n=a_1S$ for such an $S$.

A sequence of length $7$ has sum at least $2^7-1=127>95$, so $\sigma(95)\le6$. The sequence $1,2,4,8,16,64$ (ratios $2,2,2,2,4$) has sum $95$. So $\sigma(95)=6$.

**Answer: 6**

dmm-2018-power-04d.title: Rule out length 6
dmm-2018-power-04d.body:
**Basic fact.** If an SG sequence of length $m$ has ratios $k_i=a_{i+1}/a_i\ge2$, its sum is $a_1S$ with $S=1+k_1+k_1k_2+\dots+k_1\cdots k_{m-1}=1+k_1\,(1+k_2+k_2k_3+\cdots)$. So $S=1+k_1S'$ where $S'$ is the same quantity for the tail $a_2,\dots,a_m$ (length $m-1$). Since all $k_i\ge2$, $S\ge1+2+\dots+2^{m-1}=2^m-1$; in particular **a sequence of length $m$ has sum at least $2^m-1$.** Conversely, $n$ has an SG sequence of length $m$ iff $n=a_1S$ for such an $S$.

Length $7$ needs sum $\ge127>100$. Length $5$ occurs: $1,3,6,18,72$ (ratios $3,2,3,4$) has sum $100$.

For length $6$ we would need $100=a_1S$ with $S\ge63$, so $S=100$, $a_1=1$. Then $99=k_1S_5$ where $S_5\ge31$ is the value for a length-$5$ tail, $S_5\mid99$: $S_5=33$ ($k_1=3$). Then $32=k_2S_4$ with $S_4\ge15$: $S_4=16$ ($k_2=2$). Then $15=k_3S_3$ with $S_3\ge7$, but the divisors of $15$ (with $k_3\ge2$) give $S_3\in\{5,3,1\}$, all too small. So there is no length $6$ sequence and $\sigma(100)=5$.

**Answer: 5**

dmm-2018-power-05.title: Possible values of $S$
dmm-2018-power-05.body:
**Basic fact.** If an SG sequence of length $m$ has ratios $k_i=a_{i+1}/a_i\ge2$, its sum is $a_1S$ with $S=1+k_1+k_1k_2+\dots+k_1\cdots k_{m-1}=1+k_1\,(1+k_2+k_2k_3+\cdots)$. So $S=1+k_1S'$ where $S'$ is the same quantity for the tail $a_2,\dots,a_m$ (length $m-1$). Since all $k_i\ge2$, $S\ge1+2+\dots+2^{m-1}=2^m-1$; in particular **a sequence of length $m$ has sum at least $2^m-1$.** Conversely, $n$ has an SG sequence of length $m$ iff $n=a_1S$ for such an $S$.

Write $360=a_1S$. A length-$m$ sequence has $S\ge2^m-1$, $S\mid360$, and $S-1=k_1S'$ with $k_1\ge2$ and $S'$ the value of a length-$(m-1)$ tail ($S'\ge2^{m-1}-1$).

*No length $\ge6$.* Then $S\ge63$ and $S\mid360$, so $S\in\{72,90,120,180,360\}$ and $S-1\in\{71,89,119,179,359\}$. The numbers $71,89,179,359$ are prime, so $k_1=S-1$ and $S'=1$, impossible (a tail of length $\ge2$ has $S'\ge3$). For $S=120$, $119=7\cdot17$ gives $S'\in\{17,7\}$, but a tail of length $\ge5$ needs $S'\ge31$. (Length $\ge7$ would need $S\ge127$, only $180,360$, both excluded.) So $\sigma(360)\le5$.

*Length 5.* Now $S\ge31$, $S\mid360$: $S\in\{36,40,45,60,72,90,120,180,360\}$, and $S-1=k_1S_4$ with $S_4\ge15$: $S-1=35$ gives $S_4\in\{7,5\}$, $39$ gives $\{13,3\}$, $59,71,89,179,359$ are prime, $44$ gives $S_4=22$ ($k_1=2$) (the other options $11,4,2$ are too small) and $119$ gives $S_4=17$ ($k_1=7$). If $S_4=17$: $16=k_2S_3$ with $S_3\ge7$ forces $S_3=8$, but $8-1=7$ is prime, impossible for length $3$. If $S_4=22$: $21=k_2S_3$, $S_3\ge7$ forces $S_3=7$, $k_2=3$; $6=k_3S_2$ with $S_2\ge3$ forces $S_2=3$, $k_3=2$; and $S_2=1+k_4=3$ gives $k_4=2$. So the ratios are $(k_1,k_2,k_3,k_4)=(2,3,2,2)$, $S=1+2+6+12+24=45$ and $a_1=360/45=8$.

The unique sequence is $8,16,48,96,192$ (sum $360$), so $\sigma(360)=5$.

dmm-2018-power-06.title: Take $n=24$
dmm-2018-power-06.body:
**Basic fact.** If an SG sequence of length $m$ has ratios $k_i=a_{i+1}/a_i\ge2$, its sum is $a_1S$ with $S=1+k_1+k_1k_2+\dots+k_1\cdots k_{m-1}=1+k_1\,(1+k_2+k_2k_3+\cdots)$. So $S=1+k_1S'$ where $S'$ is the same quantity for the tail $a_2,\dots,a_m$ (length $m-1$). Since all $k_i\ge2$, $S\ge1+2+\dots+2^{m-1}=2^m-1$; in particular **a sequence of length $m$ has sum at least $2^m-1$.** Conversely, $n$ has an SG sequence of length $m$ iff $n=a_1S$ for such an $S$.

Note that for length $3$, $S=1+k_1(1+k_2)$ with $k_1\ge2$, $1+k_2\ge3$, so $S-1$ must be a **composite** number written as a product of a factor $\ge2$ and a factor $\ge3$; in particular $S-1$ is never prime.

*$\sigma(24)=2$.* The sequence $(1,23)$ shows $\sigma(24)\ge2$. A sequence of length $m\ge3$ has sum $24=a_1S$ with $S\ge7$, $S\mid24$, so $S\in\{8,12,24\}$ and $S-1\in\{7,11,23\}$ is prime, contradicting that $S-1=k_1S'$ with $k_1\ge2$ and $S'\ge3$. So $\sigma(24)=2$.

*Sequences.* A length-$2$ sequence is $(a,ka)$ with $a(1+k)=24$, $k\ge2$: $1+k\in\{3,4,6,8,12,24\}$ gives $(8,16),(6,18),(4,20),(3,21),(2,22),(1,23)$. These are $6\ge5$ distinct sequences of length $\sigma(24)$ with sum $24$. ∎

dmm-2018-power-07.title: Lower bound and construction
dmm-2018-power-07.body:
**Basic fact.** If an SG sequence of length $m$ has ratios $k_i=a_{i+1}/a_i\ge2$, its sum is $a_1S$ with $S=1+k_1+k_1k_2+\dots+k_1\cdots k_{m-1}=1+k_1\,(1+k_2+k_2k_3+\cdots)$. So $S=1+k_1S'$ where $S'$ is the same quantity for the tail $a_2,\dots,a_m$ (length $m-1$). Since all $k_i\ge2$, $S\ge1+2+\dots+2^{m-1}=2^m-1$; in particular **a sequence of length $m$ has sum at least $2^m-1$.** Conversely, $n$ has an SG sequence of length $m$ iff $n=a_1S$ for such an $S$.

If $\sigma(n)=k$ there is a sequence of length $k$ with sum $n$, so $n\ge2^k-1$. Conversely, $1,2,4,\dots,2^{k-1}$ has sum $2^k-1$ and length $k$, and no sequence of length $k+1$ can have sum $2^k-1<2^{k+1}-1$. Hence $\sigma(2^k-1)=k$ and the smallest $n$ is $2^k-1$.

**Answer: $2^k-1$**

dmm-2018-power-08.title: Construction and bound
dmm-2018-power-08.body:
**Basic fact.** If an SG sequence of length $m$ has ratios $k_i=a_{i+1}/a_i\ge2$, its sum is $a_1S$ with $S=1+k_1+k_1k_2+\dots+k_1\cdots k_{m-1}=1+k_1\,(1+k_2+k_2k_3+\cdots)$. So $S=1+k_1S'$ where $S'$ is the same quantity for the tail $a_2,\dots,a_m$ (length $m-1$). Since all $k_i\ge2$, $S\ge1+2+\dots+2^{m-1}=2^m-1$; in particular **a sequence of length $m$ has sum at least $2^m-1$.** Conversely, $n$ has an SG sequence of length $m$ iff $n=a_1S$ for such an $S$.

The leading digit is $1$, so the zero is in position $m$ with $0\le m\le k-2$ and $n=(2^k-1)-2^m$.

*Upper bound.* A sequence of length $k$ has sum at least $2^k-1>n$, so $\sigma(n)\le k-1$.

*Construction.* Let $a_i=2^{i-1}$ for $1\le i\le m$ and $a_i=2^i$ for $m<i\le k-1$ (ratios $2$ except one ratio $4$ at step $m\to m+1$ when $m\ge1$; for $m=0$ the sequence is $2,4,\dots,2^{k-1}$). It is an SG sequence of length $k-1$ with sum $(2^m-1)+\sum_{i=m+1}^{k-1}2^i=(2^m-1)+(2^k-2^{m+1})=2^k-1-2^m=n$. Hence $\sigma(n)=k-1$. ∎

dmm-2018-power-09.title: Sums of length-10 sequences
dmm-2018-power-09.body:
**Basic fact.** If an SG sequence of length $m$ has ratios $k_i=a_{i+1}/a_i\ge2$, its sum is $a_1S$ with $S=1+k_1+k_1k_2+\dots+k_1\cdots k_{m-1}=1+k_1\,(1+k_2+k_2k_3+\cdots)$. So $S=1+k_1S'$ where $S'$ is the same quantity for the tail $a_2,\dots,a_m$ (length $m-1$). Since all $k_i\ge2$, $S\ge1+2+\dots+2^{m-1}=2^m-1$; in particular **a sequence of length $m$ has sum at least $2^m-1$.** Conversely, $n$ has an SG sequence of length $m$ iff $n=a_1S$ for such an $S$.

A sequence of length $11$ has sum $\ge2047$, so every $n<2047$ with a length-$10$ sequence has $\sigma(n)=10$ exactly. We need the three smallest sums of length-$10$ sequences (with $a_1S$, $a_1\ge2$ giving sums $\ge2046$, we may take $a_1=1$ for small sums).

With ratios $k_1,\dots,k_9$ the sum is $S=\sum_{j=0}^{9}P_j$, $P_j=k_1\cdots k_j$. All ratios $2$ gives $1023$. Otherwise let $i$ be the first index with $k_i\ge3$. Then $P_j\ge2^{j}$ for all $j$ and $P_j\ge\frac32\cdot2^j$ for $j\ge i$, so $S\ge1023+\frac12\sum_{j=i}^{9}2^j=1023+(2^9-2^{i-1})$ where $\sum_{j=i}^{9}2^{j-1}=2^9-2^{i-1}$. For $i\le8$ this is at least $1023+384=1407$, with equality for $i=8$ exactly when $k_8=3$ and all other ratios are $2$ (sum $1407$). For $i=9$: $k_9=3$ gives $S=1023+256=1279$, and $k_9\ge4$ gives $\ge1535$.

So the length-$10$ sums below $1407$ are only $1023$ and $1279$, and $1407$ is the next. Hence $a=1279$, $b=1407$, after $1023$.

**Answer: $a=1279$, $b=1407$**

dmm-2018-power-10a.title: Prepend a 1
dmm-2018-power-10a.body: Let $a_1,\dots,a_k$ be an SG sequence of length $k=\sigma(a)$ with sum $a$. Then $1,\ ba_1,\ ba_2,\dots,ba_k$ is an SG sequence: $ba_1/1=ba_1\ge2$ is an integer ($b\ge2$), and the other ratios are unchanged. Its length is $k+1$ and its sum is $1+ba=ab+1$. Hence $\sigma(ab+1)\ge k+1>\sigma(a)$. ∎

dmm-2018-power-10b.title: Scale the sequence
dmm-2018-power-10b.body:
If $a_1,\dots,a_k$ is an SG sequence of length $\sigma(a)$ with sum $a$, then $ba_1,\dots,ba_k$ is SG (same ratios) with sum $ab$, so $\sigma(ab)\ge\sigma(a)$.

*Equality example:* $a=3,b=2$. $\sigma(3)=2$ ($1,2$). A length-$3$ sequence has sum at least $7>6$, so $\sigma(6)=2$ (as $1,5$ is SG with sum $6$). Hence $\sigma(6)=\sigma(3)$. ∎

dmm-2018-power-11.title: $\sigma(24)=2$
dmm-2018-power-11.body:
**Basic fact.** If an SG sequence of length $m$ has ratios $k_i=a_{i+1}/a_i\ge2$, its sum is $a_1S$ with $S=1+k_1+k_1k_2+\dots+k_1\cdots k_{m-1}=1+k_1\,(1+k_2+k_2k_3+\cdots)$. So $S=1+k_1S'$ where $S'$ is the same quantity for the tail $a_2,\dots,a_m$ (length $m-1$). Since all $k_i\ge2$, $S\ge1+2+\dots+2^{m-1}=2^m-1$; in particular **a sequence of length $m$ has sum at least $2^m-1$.** Conversely, $n$ has an SG sequence of length $m$ iff $n=a_1S$ for such an $S$.

Note that for length $3$, $S=1+k_1(1+k_2)$ with $k_1\ge2$, $1+k_2\ge3$, so $S-1$ must be a **composite** number written as a product of a factor $\ge2$ and a factor $\ge3$; in particular $S-1$ is never prime.

For $\sigma(24)=2$: $(1,23)$ has length $2$. A sequence of length $m\ge3$ has sum $24=a_1S$ with $S\ge7$ and $S\mid24$, so $S\in\{8,12,24\}$, but then $S-1\in\{7,11,23\}$ is prime, impossible by the note above. So $\sigma(24)=2$.

*Every $n>24$ has $\sigma(n)\ge3$.* A length-$3$ sequence with ratios $k_1,k_2$ has sum $a_1(1+k_1+k_1k_2)$. In particular $(a,2a,2ka)$ has sum $a(3+2k)$, so every number with an odd divisor $d\ge7$ (take $a=n/d$, $2k+3=d$, $k\ge2$) has a length-$3$ sequence. Similarly $(a,5a,10a)$ has sum $16a$ and $(a,3a,6a)$ has sum $10a$.

Let $n>24$. If $n$ has an odd divisor $\ge7$, done. Otherwise $n=2^j\cdot t$ with $t\in\{1,3,5\}$. If $t=1$ then $n\ge32$ so $16\mid n$. If $t=3$ then $n>24$ forces $j\ge4$ ($3\cdot16=48$) so $16\mid n$. If $t=5$ then $n=5\cdot2^j>24$ gives $j\ge1$ so $10\mid n$. In every case $\sigma(n)\ge3$. Also $\sigma(24)=2$, so the largest $n$ with $\sigma(n)=2$ is $24$.

**Answer: 24**

dmm-2018-power-12.title: Every integer above 48 has $\sigma\ge4$
dmm-2018-power-12.body:
**Basic fact.** If an SG sequence of length $m$ has ratios $k_i=a_{i+1}/a_i\ge2$, its sum is $a_1S$ with $S=1+k_1+k_1k_2+\dots+k_1\cdots k_{m-1}=1+k_1\,(1+k_2+k_2k_3+\cdots)$. So $S=1+k_1S'$ where $S'$ is the same quantity for the tail $a_2,\dots,a_m$ (length $m-1$). Since all $k_i\ge2$, $S\ge1+2+\dots+2^{m-1}=2^m-1$; in particular **a sequence of length $m$ has sum at least $2^m-1$.** Conversely, $n$ has an SG sequence of length $m$ iff $n=a_1S$ for such an $S$.

Since $24n\ge72>48$, the claim follows from the following theorem (which also settles Problem 13).

**Theorem.** Every integer $n>48$ has $\sigma(n)\ge4$.

Call $d$ *good* if there is an SG sequence of length $4$ with sum $d$. If $d$ is good and $d\mid n$, multiplying that sequence by $n/d$ gives a length-$4$ SG sequence with sum $n$, so $\sigma(n)\ge4$. Hence it is enough to show that every $n>48$ is divisible by a good number.

**Step 1: every prime $p\ge19$ is good.** If $p\equiv3\pmod4$, use $1,2,4,p-7$ (ratios $2,2,\frac{p-7}4\ge3$). If $p\equiv1\pmod4$ with $p<53$: $29$: $1,4,8,16$; $37$: $1,4,8,24$; $41$: $1,4,12,24$. If $p=4u+1\ge53$ (so $u\ge13$):
- $u$ odd: $1,4,8,4u-12$ (ratios $4,2,\frac{u-3}2\ge5$), sum $4u+1$;
- $u=2v$ with $v$ odd ($v\ge7$): $1,8,16,8v-24$ (ratios $8,2,\frac{v-3}2\ge2$), sum $1+8+16+8v-24=8v+1=p$;
- $4\mid u$: $1,\frac u4,\frac{3u}4,3u$ (ratios $\frac u4\ge4,3,4$), sum $1+4u=p$.

**Step 2: a table.** The following numbers are good, by the sequences shown: $15$: $1,2,4,8$; $21$: $1,2,6,12$; $22$: $1,3,6,12$; $27$: $1,2,4,20$; $28$: $1,3,6,18$; $29$: $1,4,8,16$; $33$: $1,2,6,24$; $34$: $1,3,6,24$; $35$: $1,2,4,28$; $36$: $1,5,10,20$; $37$: $1,4,8,24$; $39$: $1,2,4,32$; $40$: $1,3,6,30$; $41$: $1,4,12,24$; $49$: $1,3,9,36$; $50$: $1,7,14,28$; $51$: $1,2,4,44$; $52$: $1,3,6,42$; $55$: $1,2,4,48$; $64$: $1,3,6,54$; $65$: $1,4,12,48$; $77$: $1,4,8,64$; $85$: $1,3,9,72$; $91$: $1,2,4,84$; $96$: $1,5,10,80$; $119$: $1,2,4,112$; $121$: $1,3,9,108$; $125$: $1,4,8,112$; $143$: $1,2,4,136$; $169$: $1,3,15,150$; $187$: $1,2,4,180$; $221$: $1,4,8,208$; $289$: $1,2,22,264$.

**Step 3.** Let $n>48$. If $n$ has a prime factor $\ge19$, it is divisible by a good prime (Step 1). Otherwise all prime factors lie in $\{2,3,5,7,11,13,17\}$.
- If two different odd primes $p<q$ divide $n$, then $pq\in\{15,21,33,39,51,35,55,65,85,77,91,119,143,187,221\}$ divides $n$, and all of these are good.
- Otherwise $n=2^a p^b$ with $p$ an odd prime $\le17$ or $b=0$.
  - $b=0$: $n=2^a>48$ gives $a\ge6$, so $64\mid n$.
  - $p=3$: if $b\ge3$ then $27\mid n$; if $b=2$ then $a\ge2$ (since $n>48$) and $36\mid n$; if $b=1$ then $a\ge5$ and $96\mid n$.
  - $p=5$: if $b\ge3$ then $125\mid n$; if $b=2$ then $a\ge1$ and $50\mid n$; if $b=1$ then $a\ge4$ and $40\mid n$.
  - $p=7$: if $b\ge2$ then $49\mid n$; if $b=1$ then $a\ge3$ and $28\mid n$.
  - $p=11$: if $b\ge2$ then $121\mid n$; if $b=1$ then $a\ge1$ and $22\mid n$.
  - $p=13$: if $b\ge2$ then $169\mid n$; if $b=1$ then $a\ge2$ and $52\mid n$.
  - $p=17$: if $b\ge2$ then $289\mid n$; if $b=1$ then $a\ge1$ and $34\mid n$.

In every case $n$ is divisible by a good number, so $\sigma(n)\ge4>3$. ∎

dmm-2018-power-13.title: Every integer above 48 has $\sigma\ge4$
dmm-2018-power-13.body:
**Basic fact.** If an SG sequence of length $m$ has ratios $k_i=a_{i+1}/a_i\ge2$, its sum is $a_1S$ with $S=1+k_1+k_1k_2+\dots+k_1\cdots k_{m-1}=1+k_1\,(1+k_2+k_2k_3+\cdots)$. So $S=1+k_1S'$ where $S'$ is the same quantity for the tail $a_2,\dots,a_m$ (length $m-1$). Since all $k_i\ge2$, $S\ge1+2+\dots+2^{m-1}=2^m-1$; in particular **a sequence of length $m$ has sum at least $2^m-1$.** Conversely, $n$ has an SG sequence of length $m$ iff $n=a_1S$ for such an $S$.

We prove the stronger statement that $\sigma(n)\ge4$ for **every** $n>48$ (with or without the condition $24\nmid n$).

**Theorem.** Every integer $n>48$ has $\sigma(n)\ge4$.

Call $d$ *good* if there is an SG sequence of length $4$ with sum $d$. If $d$ is good and $d\mid n$, multiplying that sequence by $n/d$ gives a length-$4$ SG sequence with sum $n$, so $\sigma(n)\ge4$. Hence it is enough to show that every $n>48$ is divisible by a good number.

**Step 1: every prime $p\ge19$ is good.** If $p\equiv3\pmod4$, use $1,2,4,p-7$ (ratios $2,2,\frac{p-7}4\ge3$). If $p\equiv1\pmod4$ with $p<53$: $29$: $1,4,8,16$; $37$: $1,4,8,24$; $41$: $1,4,12,24$. If $p=4u+1\ge53$ (so $u\ge13$):
- $u$ odd: $1,4,8,4u-12$ (ratios $4,2,\frac{u-3}2\ge5$), sum $4u+1$;
- $u=2v$ with $v$ odd ($v\ge7$): $1,8,16,8v-24$ (ratios $8,2,\frac{v-3}2\ge2$), sum $1+8+16+8v-24=8v+1=p$;
- $4\mid u$: $1,\frac u4,\frac{3u}4,3u$ (ratios $\frac u4\ge4,3,4$), sum $1+4u=p$.

**Step 2: a table.** The following numbers are good, by the sequences shown: $15$: $1,2,4,8$; $21$: $1,2,6,12$; $22$: $1,3,6,12$; $27$: $1,2,4,20$; $28$: $1,3,6,18$; $29$: $1,4,8,16$; $33$: $1,2,6,24$; $34$: $1,3,6,24$; $35$: $1,2,4,28$; $36$: $1,5,10,20$; $37$: $1,4,8,24$; $39$: $1,2,4,32$; $40$: $1,3,6,30$; $41$: $1,4,12,24$; $49$: $1,3,9,36$; $50$: $1,7,14,28$; $51$: $1,2,4,44$; $52$: $1,3,6,42$; $55$: $1,2,4,48$; $64$: $1,3,6,54$; $65$: $1,4,12,48$; $77$: $1,4,8,64$; $85$: $1,3,9,72$; $91$: $1,2,4,84$; $96$: $1,5,10,80$; $119$: $1,2,4,112$; $121$: $1,3,9,108$; $125$: $1,4,8,112$; $143$: $1,2,4,136$; $169$: $1,3,15,150$; $187$: $1,2,4,180$; $221$: $1,4,8,208$; $289$: $1,2,22,264$.

**Step 3.** Let $n>48$. If $n$ has a prime factor $\ge19$, it is divisible by a good prime (Step 1). Otherwise all prime factors lie in $\{2,3,5,7,11,13,17\}$.
- If two different odd primes $p<q$ divide $n$, then $pq\in\{15,21,33,39,51,35,55,65,85,77,91,119,143,187,221\}$ divides $n$, and all of these are good.
- Otherwise $n=2^a p^b$ with $p$ an odd prime $\le17$ or $b=0$.
  - $b=0$: $n=2^a>48$ gives $a\ge6$, so $64\mid n$.
  - $p=3$: if $b\ge3$ then $27\mid n$; if $b=2$ then $a\ge2$ (since $n>48$) and $36\mid n$; if $b=1$ then $a\ge5$ and $96\mid n$.
  - $p=5$: if $b\ge3$ then $125\mid n$; if $b=2$ then $a\ge1$ and $50\mid n$; if $b=1$ then $a\ge4$ and $40\mid n$.
  - $p=7$: if $b\ge2$ then $49\mid n$; if $b=1$ then $a\ge3$ and $28\mid n$.
  - $p=11$: if $b\ge2$ then $121\mid n$; if $b=1$ then $a\ge1$ and $22\mid n$.
  - $p=13$: if $b\ge2$ then $169\mid n$; if $b=1$ then $a\ge2$ and $52\mid n$.
  - $p=17$: if $b\ge2$ then $289\mid n$; if $b=1$ then $a\ge1$ and $34\mid n$.

In every case $n$ is divisible by a good number, so $\sigma(n)\ge4>3$. ∎
